DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
The paper proposes two changes for 1 April:
- **Raise three prices:** fish and chips +£1, the burger +£1, sirloin steak +£2, worth a projected £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in extra gross profit.
- **Remove the mushroom risotto**, on the grounds that it has "the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales."

The till data and competitor check are a good basis, and the price increases themselves look reasonable. But the case for removing the risotto is contradicted by Table 1, and the projection leaves out the 12% beef cost rise that the paper itself reports. The likely effect of VAT matters too.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest

| Dish | Gross margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80% (highest)** | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Specials | 64% | — |
| Sirloin steak | 60% (lowest) | £15.60 |

- The paper and your description both call the risotto's margin the weakest. Table 1 shows it is the strongest.
- Its sales, at 90 plates a week, are tied lowest with specials.
- **Replacing it is likely to cost money.** A replacement special at £14, at the current specials margin of 64%, would earn £8.96 a plate instead of £11.20. That is about **£200 a week (around £10,500 a year) less**, cancelling roughly a quarter of the price-increase gain.
- It is probably also your main vegetarian option, so removing it carries a risk with any group booking that includes a vegetarian.

## 2. The beef cost rise isn't in the projection

§4 reports beef rising 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. The paper doesn't give each dish's beef cost, so here is a range:

| | If all food cost is beef (upper bound) | If beef is about half the burger's cost |
|---|---|---|
| Steak (£10.40 a plate) | +£1.25 × 120 = £150 a week | £150 a week |
| Burger (£4.20 a plate) | +£0.50 × 260 = £130 a week | about £65 a week |
| **Total** | **about £280 a week** | **about £215 a week** |

- That reduces the £810 gain by about a quarter to a third.
- **The steak's margin falls even after its £2 increase:** (£28.00 − £11.65) / £28.00 = 58%, against 60% now.

## 3. VAT probably needs to come out

UK menu prices include VAT at 20%, and all of the paper's figures appear to be calculated on menu prices.

- **Gross profit:** of each £1 price increase, about £0.83 is extra takings for the restaurant. The £810 a week becomes about **£675** after VAT.
- **Margins:** a margin calculated on the price including VAT overstates the true margin. Fish and chips is 69% as stated, but about 63% on the price excluding VAT.

Check how the 70% target in §1 is measured. If it's on prices excluding VAT, as is usual, the paper's margins aren't comparable to it.

## 4. What this does to the projection

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| As stated | £810 | £42,120 |
| After VAT | £675 | £35,100 |
| Less beef rise (about £215–280 before VAT, about £180–235 after) | about £440–495 | about £23,000–26,000 |
| Less removing the risotto (about £200 before VAT, about £170 after) | about £270–325 | **about £14,000–17,000** |

The "about 71%" main-course margin is correct on the paper's own basis: excluding specials and before beef, it rises from 69.9% to 71.3%. Including the beef rise, it is about 70%. Excluding VAT, it is lower still.

## 5. Further points

- **Trading days.** §2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. The recommendation says "six trading days." The projection uses weeks, so the figures aren't affected, but the text should be consistent. Multiplying by 52 also assumes no weeks closed.
- **The volume assumption.** A 60% repeat-booking rate shows loyalty. It doesn't show how customers react to price. The 2024 evidence covers bookings, not dish choice. Guests might keep coming but switch from steak to curry, for example. Watch the mix of dishes, not just total plates.
- **Monitoring.** The January–February baseline is a winter period. April–May will differ seasonally anyway, so compare with the same weeks last year. Also set a trigger: what fall in sales of a dish would lead you to reverse its increase?
- **Competitor check.** It's useful, but it doesn't cover curry or risotto.

## 6. What holds up

- **The arithmetic:** all margins, the 1,050 total, the £810 weekly gain and the £42,120 annual figure are calculated correctly.
- **Competitor positioning:** each new price stays below the competitor midpoint (fish £17.98, burger £16.50, steak £29.50).
- **The case for raising prices:** overall margin fell from 70% to 67%, and prices haven't changed since September 2024.
- **The choice of dishes to increase:** they are priced lowest against competitors and have the highest volumes.

## 7. What is settled and what is open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- the risotto has the highest margin, not the weakest;
- the projection leaves out the beef cost rise reported in §4;
- after the price rise, the steak's margin falls below its current level once beef is included.

**Open, and what would settle each question:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Whether figures include VAT | How the margins and the 70% target are calculated |
| Beef cost per plate | The kitchen's recipe costings for steak and burger |
| The replacement special's margin | A costed recipe for the planned special |
| Whether customers switch dishes | Weekly sales by dish, compared year on year |

## 8. Suggested revision to the recommendations

> We recommend raising fish and chips to £17.50, the burger to £16.00 and sirloin steak to £28.00 from 1 April. After the 12% beef cost increase and VAT, this adds an estimated £23,000–26,000 a year in gross profit; final figures depend on beef recipe costings. We recommend **keeping** the mushroom risotto, which has the highest margin on the menu (80%). We will monitor weekly sales by dish against the same weeks in 2025, and review any dish whose sales fall by more than [X]%.

I can rebuild Table 1 showing new prices, beef-adjusted costs and margins excluding VAT, if that would help.
